claims.text: Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling induces high lattice strain in CoCrFeNiTi powder.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling produces a CoCrFeNiTi grain size below 20 nm.
Milling-induced strain and grain refinement lower the thermodynamic energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC transition.
SPS at 1000°C for 5–10 minutes and 50–60 MPa will produce greater than 98% density.
SPS at 1000°C with a short dwell will avoid excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
The VEC of CoCrFeNiTi is approximately 7.0–7.5.
The atomic-radius mismatch of CoCrFeNiTi is below 6.5%.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the stability of the proposed BCC phase in CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling-induced lattice strain raises the chemical potential of the FCC phase.
Thermal energy supplied by SPS overcomes the remaining kinetic barrier for BCC formation and densification.
A short dwell at 1000°C prevents sufficient Ti segregation and HCP nucleation.
The resulting alloy will have a single BCC or BCC+FCC solid-solution structure.
The SPS alloy will have higher Vickers hardness because of grain-boundary strengthening and solid-solution effects.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi alloys typically have low hardness and high porosity.
Slow cooling and the absence of milling-induced strain cause cast CoCrFeNiTi to contain mixed FCC/BCC phases and potential Ti-rich HCP precipitates.
Above approximately 1050°C, Ti diffusion causes excessive HCP precipitation and grain coarsening.
Milling for less than 4 hours is insufficient to generate the critical strain needed to shift phase stability toward BCC.
Ti dissolution may lag behind that of the other elements because of its high melting point, producing local chemical inhomogeneity.
Residual oxygen can alter the threshold temperature for HCP precipitation.
Low-load Vickers testing at 10–25 g can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The boundary predicts that 1100°C should increase HCP formation relative to 1000°C, but the falsification rule treats that same increase as falsifying rather than supporting the proposed temperature boundary.

The boundary predicts that less than 4 hours of milling is insufficient; therefore, failure of the 3-hour sample to show BCC dominance or increased hardness would support the hypothesis, yet the falsification rule labels it as falsification.

The structural mediator invokes rapid diffusion kinetics to suppress Ti-rich HCP nucleation, whereas the mechanism attributes HCP suppression to limiting Ti segregation and diffusion through a short dwell. These are opposing accounts of the relevant diffusion behavior.
